title: Climate shock becomes economic adaptation
subtitle: Gulf of Maine, 1815–1820
description: Historical export and temperature analysis links unusual conditions to inferred fish responses and changing fishing effort. Dams, trade reopening, markets and population also matter; their relative contributions require further review.

title: Weather shock becomes a subsistence crisis
subtitle: Czech Lands, 1816–1817
description: Cold and wet weather damaged crops and contributed to grain-price pressure into 1817. Crop differences, postwar demand and market conditions complicate attribution.

title: Cold years store risk in the water system
subtitle: Alpine Rhine Basin, 1816–1817
description: Cold conditions formed the background to substantial snow storage. The model favors fresh spring 1817 snowfall over enduring 1816 snow as flood meltwater, combined with intense rainfall that the reconstruction underestimates.

title: Climate becomes cultural context
subtitle: Geneva, summer 1816
description: Stormy Geneva weather forms part of the reported setting for Frankenstein’s conception. The ghost-story challenge, scientific debates and Mary Shelley’s creative choices are additional influences; manuscript dates establish drafting chronology.

title: The same volcanic forcing, a different regional expression
subtitle: Qing China, 1815–1816
description: Southern Chinese documents report unusual cold in 1815–1816. Temperature and hydroclimate reconstructions differ spatially; regional variation and proxy disagreement remain part of the evidence.

title: Direct eruption damage disrupts local livelihoods
subtitle: Sumbawa, 1815–1819 context
description: Direct food and water damage and later maritime difficulty are distinct branches. Long-term recovery remains only partly documented.
